newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Holocaust victims ignored when Swiss wealth seized.
newsitem.headline: Holocaust victims ignored when Swiss wealth seized.

text.p: Wealth stashed in Switzerland by Jews killed in the Holocaust was sucked into a world of high-powered postwar politics that held little regard for the money's original owners, documents emerging from archives show.

Previously secret accords show Switzerland quietly agreed to hand over East European Jews' unclaimed wealth as part of deals with Poland and Hungary compensating Swiss citizens for property nationalised by communist regimes there after the war.

But Peter Hug, a historian who has studied the postwar pacts, said they simply reflected international private law that holds any property for which private heirs cannot be found belongs to the country in which the original owner last lived.
This does not change the fact, however, that the original owners or their heirs still have every right to the money.

"The decisive point is that the rights of the original owners are completely intact up to the present day. These rights have not changed at all. In my view, it is a secondary matter who actually administers the funds today," he said.
"The pressing moral question that arises is: how much did the administrators do to find the owners, and there I would say there were big shortcomings.

"They did not do everything humanly possible -- neither Switzerland, nor private asset administrators, nor the Polish state, nor Hungary -- to find these rightful owners. That is the problem, and this must be remedied."
Switzerland also struck a deal with the western Allies in 1946 calling on Berne to check how it could hand over dormant accounts to the Allies for distribution to Holocaust victims.
"This was never done," Hug said, because the Swiss government split over the issue and the western Allies never pressed the point.
"Why did the western Allies simply forget? Why did they not insist?" he asked.

"My impression is that this -- very much more than the Swiss themselves would like -- was a subject of international politics and not national policy. This was based on mutual agreements and understandings that one hand washed the other. Who was left behind? The rightful owners."
The leader of Switzerland's Jewish community, Rolf Bloch, said this week it was "indefensible" to use Holocaust accounts to help Eastern European countries compensate Swiss citizens.
And World Jewish Congress President Edgar Bronfman has vowed to take the fight over the Swiss assets to other nations of Western Europe to make sure Jews are not abused again.

"This is not just about money," he told Jewish leaders in New York on Wednesday. "It is about Jewish dignity, Jewish rights, Jewish feelings, about being Jewish, about the fact that we are not going to be pushed around any more."
Hug said Jewish groups who accused Switzerland of robbing Holocaust victims were missing the point.
"They don't understand the mechanism," he said, noting Poland and Hungary were legally entitled to their citizens' unclaimed assets in Switzerland.
What deserved criticism is the apparent willingness of countries to keep the wealth away from its original owners.
Hug noted the Swiss government refused to hand over to Poland a list naming the original owners of unclaimed Polish assets that Berne gave Warsaw under their 1949 accord.

This made it impossible for Poland to return to any survivors some 480,000 Swiss francs it got under the pact, even if it wanted to. Poland is still liable for these funds should any survivors come forward, Hug said.

He said dormant assets that were never reported to the Swiss government remain the liability of Swiss banks and insurers that hold the money, while the Swiss government is liable for funds it called in under a 1962 decree and put in a special account.
Switzerland is also responsible for 325,000 francs in dormant assets it earmarked for Hungary under a similar accord.
